analysis.one_liner: Suspends the federal gasoline tax through 2023 and taxes oil companies' excess profits at 50%.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have cut the federal gasoline tax and taxed large oil companies' excess profits, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set the federal gasoline tax to zero — a cut of about 18 cents per gallon at the pump — from enactment through December 31, 2023, and replaced the lost Highway Trust Fund money with general Treasury funds so road programs were not shortchanged. It would also have imposed a 50% tax on the excess profits of large integrated oil companies, measured against their 2015-2019 average profit plus 10%. It never got a hearing in the Ways and Means Committee and expired at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and anyone who buys gasoline, who would pay up to about 18 cents a gallon less for roughly 18 months; the federal portion of the pump price would be suspended entirely for that period. Highway programs would be held harmless because the bill directs the Treasury to treat the lost fuel-tax revenue as if it had been collected. The bill also declares it the sense of Congress that producers and dealers must pass the tax cut straight through to customers, including immediate credits to customer accounts.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the federal excise tax on gasoline to zero cents per gallon from enactment through December 31, 2023, suspending the roughly 18-cent federal charge included in the pump price.
Replaces the lost Highway Trust Fund and Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund revenue dollar-for-dollar from general Treasury funds, so road and cleanup programs do not lose money.

Imposes a 50% fee on the excess profits of integrated oil companies — profits above their average 2015-2019 adjusted taxable income plus 10% — so large oil companies, which recorded record profits during the 2022 price spike, would partly finance the tax cut and pay a share of windfall earnings.

Includes floor-stock refunds for dealers and a sense of Congress that consumers immediately receive the benefit, designed to force the tax cut through to pump prices rather than letting sellers keep it.

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil companies, which would owe a 50% tax on profits above their pre-pandemic baseline. The federal Treasury would also absorb the cost of replacing the suspended gas tax revenue, adding to the deficit for the duration of the suspension.
analysis.who_pays_short: Integrated oil companies and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: A gas tax suspension does not guarantee savings at the pump: if wholesale prices do not fall, refiners and dealers can keep the 18 cents per gallon. The bill can only urge pass-through through a non-binding sense of Congress and dealer refund certifications.

Replacing the suspended Highway Trust Fund revenue with general Treasury funds would add roughly $10-20 billion to the federal deficit during the suspension period, rather than having road users fund the roads.

A one-time 50% windfall tax on oil company profits could discourage investment in new supply, which some economists argue would keep prices higher over time — the counterargument supporters of such taxes dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct consumer benefit is real but modest — up to about 18 cents a gallon, and only if sellers pass it through, which the bill can encourage but not guarantee. The windfall tax targets a narrow set of large oil companies at a moment of record profits, which recaptures some of the cost, but the deficit-financed trust fund replacement and the pass-through problem are genuine design weaknesses. On balance it is a consumer-relief bill with a financing mechanism that leans on oil majors and the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on May 31, 2022, during a period of high gasoline prices.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, which is the last action ever taken on it.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill.
The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 without coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies are better off because the bill died: they never faced the 50% tax on profits above their 2015-2019 baseline. Drivers never got the federal tax holiday either, since no competing version advanced.

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no report of the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the only member to sign on was its Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: They would owe a 50% fee on profits above their 2015-2019 average plus 10%, clawing back part of the windfall earnings they recorded during the 2022 price spike. Keeping that revenue is their gain and the public's cost.

They would collect the suspended tax on inventories as refunds but would be pressed by the bill's floor-stock rules and sense of Congress to pass the full 18 cents per gallon through to customers rather than keeping it.
The trust fund would not lose money: the bill directs the Treasury to treat the lost gas tax revenue as collected, keeping highway funding whole while drivers pay less.
